19. **The living map.** (added 29 October 2026) Haakon: "In time I want environmental effects, seasons reflected on the map. Characters, armies, fighting shown, etc. Everything you can think of, which makes it a better game for a player or viewer. But I don't believe the time for these effects are quiet yet." With every feature built, the map's look becomes a blend of Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age world ("The map in true geography, and its look in time" under Interface): the environment and the seasons on the map, characters, armies and battles as they travel and fight, every unit and figure drawn after the period's own relics in its culture's idiom, a map that remembers the war, life drawn from the simulation, every level of what is built (roads by quality, harbours and docks, walls, water works, granaries, mines), a seasonal year, each realm's own map drawn by its scribes, omens in the margin and small scenes at big moments, and whatever else makes the game better to play or to watch, each measured on a throttled phone. Presentation only, with no change to rules, numbers or balance, so it may run beside item 18. **Stop for review.** Then **19+, answers to 19's review** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "Yes to all"): each realm's own map pressed in clay for every court that writes cuneiform, as the period's clay maps were, and on papyrus for Egypt; a sacked city stays in ruins until its people come back, and they come back by the rule that already moves them ("Feeding a province draws its people": settled people move towards more room, measured in food, and the loose drift towards richer land), so the ruins fade as its people return and its walls are rebuilt with item 15's works, with no rule for rebuilding (Haakon: "no special rules for cities recovering, people will migrate back at the harvest potential difference there becomes bigger than neighboring cities"); and Egypt's view gets hieratic notes as decoration only, the map's own text staying in the reader's language. Presentation only. Then **19++, the visual pass** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "I also think amarna letters needs another visual pass. With the instructions to make it as visually impressive as it possibly can, without tanking the performance."): every screen, not only the map, made as impressive as it can be: the map at every zoom, the province card, the seat view, the letters and their tablets, the council, the chronicle, replay and god view, menus and the first screen, in light and dark, on phone and desktop. One look throughout, in the style the living map set (Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age, each culture drawn in its own idiom after the period's relics), with type, colour, texture, light, motion and the small touches that make a game feel crafted, never clutter that hides what a king needs to read. The bound is that it stays playable on a phone (Haakon: "Well, it can get slower, but must be playable on a phone. That's the criteria."): measured as item 19 measures it, on a throttled phone in the busiest scene of each screen, smooth enough to read and play and to watch at top speed without falling behind, with reduced motion respected; it may cost more than now where it buys something worth seeing. The pass starts by finding every graphical glitch and inconsistency on every screen (Haakon: "There are also many graphical glitches and Inconsistencies in the game right now."): things drawn wrong, out of place, overlapping or flickering, and the same thing drawn or named differently in two places; each is listed in the PR with its picture and fixed. The PR shows every screen before and after at 390 px and desktop 2x, light and dark, with the performance numbers before and after. Presentation only, so it may run beside item 18. Then **19+++, the music** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "Would love if we could make something properly similar in that style instead (choir, strings, reed and drums) around the Hurrian Hymn, that actually sounds good. \[...\] And have the music be dynamic exactly like it is in Empire Earth. \[...\] the music is same for all you play, but should be dynamic in the same way as Empire Earth, with the few variations on the pieces, and each piece playing according to the situation. Use the Empire Earth pieces as the template, and make as many as Empire Earth had, each inspired by each piece there, expertly."). The game has no music or sound yet. First the template: list Empire Earth's pieces from its sources, how many there are, the mood and role of each and when the game played it, and how its dynamic music chose and changed pieces with the situation. Then as many pieces of our own, one for each of Empire Earth's, each taking that piece's role, mood, pace and colour (a solemn choir, warm strings, a solo reed, frame drums and the period's lyres, harps and pipes) and nothing that is that piece's own: no melody, no recognisable progression or line, since those belong to their owners; the melodies come from the Hurrian Hymn of Ugarit (about 1400 BCE, free to use, read from its scholarly reconstructions) and from new themes in the Babylonian tunings, so the game has one musical voice, the same for every court. Each piece has a few variations, and the music is dynamic as Empire Earth's was: the situation of the seat being played (or the whole map in god view) picks the piece, calm, rising tension, war, siege, battle, triumph, loss and the age's last seasons, changing at a phrase's end, never the same variation twice running. It must sound good, not merely correct: composed as scores, rendered offline with orchestral and choir samples whose licences allow their rendered sound in a free, open game (CC0 or as free, each licence recorded), mixed and mastered to one loudness, and shipped as compressed audio loaded on demand so the first screen stays fast and the phone stays playable. And a sound design in the manner of Crusader Kings II (Haakon, 30 October 2026: "And sound effect can be inspired by CK2?", then, to the design session's take, "Yes, please, expertly!"), its approach and feel, nothing from its files: every action and event has its own short sound in the period's terms, so a player hears what happened without looking (the stylus pressed into clay as a letter is written, a cylinder seal rolled, a tablet set in its envelope, gold weighed on the scales, a courier's arrival, Egypt's trumpets or a war horn when war is declared, the sistrum for a temple or an omen, a lyre's phrase when an envoy is received); restrained, short and soft, each with a few slight variations so it never tires; a quiet bed of the world under the music that follows what the map shows (the Nile's water, the steppe's wind, a city's market, a siege camp); and a short sting for the great moments (a capital falling, a king's death, the age's end) before the music takes them up. Quiet by default, with music and sound switches remembered between visits. Haakon judges by ear: the PR has a listening page with every piece and variation, and the template's list beside it; any piece he dislikes is redone before it merges. Presentation only.
